'''Catherine D. Nobes''' (born 1 April 1964) is a Professor of Cell Biology and Head of School of Biochemistry at the [[University of Bristol]]. She studies the regulation of cell migration and invasion of cancer cells by [[Eph receptor|Eph receptors]].

== Early life and education ==
Nobes went to school at [[Windsor Girls' School]] and was a county level [[high jump|high jumper]] as a teenager{{Citation needed|date=May 2019}}. She studied biochemistry at the [[University of London]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.bristol.ac.uk/biochemistry/news/2014/outputurl-86374-en.html|title=2014: outputurl-86374-en. {{!}} School of Biochemistry {{!}} University of Bristol|last=Bristol|first=University of|website=www.bristol.ac.uk|language=en-GB|access-date=2019-01-10}}</ref> She completed a PhD at the [[University of Cambridge]], working with Martin Brand. Nobes did brief Post-Docs in [[Helen Saibil]] and Aviva Tolkovsky's labs in Oxford before joining [[Alan Hall]]'s laboratory at the [[University College London]], where she identified the role of the [[GTPase]] [[CDC42]] and effectors in forming [[actin]]-rich [[Filopodia|filopodial]] extensions.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Self|first1=A.|last2=Etienne-Manneville|first2=S.|date=2015-06-18|title=Alan Hall (1952-2015), an Englishman in New York|journal=The EMBO Journal|volume=34|issue=13|pages=1735–1736|doi=10.15252/embj.201570020|issn=0261-4189|pmc=4516425|pmid=26089021}}</ref> She investigated the regulation of actin [[Polymerization|polymerisation]] and how cell movement determines polarity and adhesion.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6y3VDQAAQBAJ&q=Kate+Nobes&pg=PA161|title=The Actin Cytoskeleton|last=Jockusch|first=Brigitte M.|date=2017-01-03|publisher=Springer|isbn=9783319463711|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hall|first1=Alan|last2=Nobes|first2=Catherine D.|date=1999-03-22|title=Rho GTPases Control Polarity, Protrusion, and Adhesion during Cell Movement|journal=The Journal of Cell Biology|language=en|volume=144|issue=6|pages=1235–1244|doi=10.1083/jcb.144.6.1235|issn=1540-8140|pmid=10087266|pmc=2150589}}</ref> She was awarded a [[Lister Institute of Preventive Medicine]] Fellowship in 2007, which allowed her to study cell migration in the context of axonal guidance and cancer metastasis.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NvcsETBw0o8C&q=Kate+Nobes&pg=PA449|title=Regulators and Effectors of Small GTPases, Part D: Rho Family|date=2000-10-11|publisher=Elsevier|isbn=9780080496801|language=en}}</ref>

== Research and career ==
Nobes was awarded a [[Medical Research Council (United Kingdom)|Medical Research Council]] Fellowship at [[University College London]] in 2001, where she worked in the Laboratory for Molecular Cell Biology (LMCB).<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.ucl.ac.uk/lmcb/alumni-0|title=Alumni|last=UCL|date=2015-09-30|website=UCL|language=en|access-date=2019-01-10}}</ref> Her work was featured in a [[Wellcome Trust]] exhibition of art and science, ''Growth and Form''.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/2/hi/science/nature/1192358.stm|title=Beautiful science inspires artists|date=2001-02-28|access-date=2019-01-10|language=en-GB}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Science|first=American Association for the Advancement of|date=2001-03-09|title=NetWatch: Best of the Web in science.|url=http://science.sciencemag.org/content/291/5510/netwatch|journal=Science|language=en|volume=291|issue=5510|pages=1865|issn=1095-9203}}</ref> She joined the [[University of Bristol]] as a Reader in 2006, and was promoted to a Professor of Cell Biology in 2012.<ref name=":0" /> She delivered her inaugural lecture in 2014, discussing cell migration and metastasis of cancer cells.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.bristol.ac.uk/pace/public-events/inaugural/2014/nobes.html|title=Professor Kate Nobes - inaugural lecture {{!}} Public and Ceremonial Events Office {{!}} University of Bristol|last=Bristol|first=University of|website=www.bristol.ac.uk|language=en-GB|access-date=2019-01-10}}</ref> Since 2014 she has been the head of the School of Biochemistry, the first woman to do so in the School's 50-year history.

Her work largely considers the social behaviour of [[Tumor cell|tumor cells]] in the tumor [[Microenvironment (biology)|microenvironment]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|url=http://www.bris.ac.uk/biochemistry/people/catherine-d-nobes/index.html|title=Professor Catherine Nobes - Biochemistry|last=Bristol|first=University of|website=www.bris.ac.uk|language=en-GB|access-date=2019-01-10}}</ref> She studies how colliding cells that come in to contact with each other stop migrating toward their partner, repolarise and move away from one another - a process known as [[contact inhibition]] of locomotion.<ref name=":1" /> She has studied how this cell behaviour is regulated by Eph-[[ephrin]] signalling.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=BATSON|first1=J.|last2=ASTIN|first2=J.W.|last3=NOBES|first3=C.D.|date=2013-03-15|title=Regulation of contact inhibition of locomotion by Eph-ephrin signalling|journal=Journal of Microscopy|volume=251|issue=3|pages=232–241|doi=10.1111/jmi.12024|pmid=23495724|pmc=3838626|issn=0022-2720}}</ref> Eph receptors are part of the [[Receptor tyrosine kinase|receptor tyrosine kinases]]; with two main families - EphA and EphB.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Nobes|first1=Catherine D.|last2=Campbell|first2=Jessica|last3=Taylor|first3=Hannah|date=2017-02-06|title=Ephs and ephrins|journal=Current Biology|language=English|volume=27|issue=3|pages=R90–R95|doi=10.1016/j.cub.2017.01.003|issn=0960-9822|pmid=28171762|doi-access=free|hdl=1983/948dd409-03ad-4160-a7f5-7e8838558269|hdl-access=free}}</ref> Nobes showed that in [[metastatic prostate cancer]] cells, EphB receptors are misregulated in ways that might lead to cancer cell invasion / metastasis.<ref name=":1" /> She showed that similar activation of Eph signalling may underpin epithelial cell loosening during wound healing.

=== Academic service ===
Nobes has served on the grant allocation board of the [[Royal Society]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://royalsociety.org/people/kate-nobes-12676/|title=Kate Nobes {{!}} Royal Society|website=royalsociety.org|language=en-gb|access-date=2019-01-10}}</ref> She was the editor of the [[British Society for Cell Biology]] newsletter.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://bscb.org/winter-newsletter-2013/|title=BSCB Newsletter, Winter 2013 {{!}} British Society for Cell Biology|last=administrator|language=en-US|access-date=2019-01-10}}</ref> In 2018 she joined the Advisory Committee of the [[Lister Institute of Preventive Medicine]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.lister-institute.org.uk/the-new-lister-institute-scientific-advisory-committee/|title=The New Lister Institute Scientific Advisory Committee|date=2018-05-20|website=Lister Institute|access-date=2019-01-10}}</ref>
